blocks.heading: Arguments and inference
blocks.text: An argument consists of premises and a conclusion. Premises are statements accepted as true for the argument. A conclusion is the statement being supported. A rule of inference is a valid pattern that preserves truth from premises to conclusion.

blocks.heading: Argument example
blocks.text:
Premise 1: All birds have wings.
Premise 2: A parrot is a bird.
Conclusion: A parrot has wings.

The conclusion follows by applying the general statement to the specific bird. The symbol ∴ means “therefore.”

blocks.heading: Modus Ponens
blocks.text: Modus Ponens affirms the hypothesis. p → q p ∴ q If it rains, the ground is wet. It rains. Therefore, the ground is wet.

blocks.heading: Modus Tollens
blocks.text: Modus Tollens denies the conclusion. p → q ¬q ∴ ¬p If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is not wet. Therefore, it is not raining.

blocks.heading: Hypothetical Syllogism
blocks.text: Hypothetical Syllogism chains conditionals. p → q q → r ∴ p → r If it rains, the ground is wet. If the ground is wet, the grass is slippery. Therefore, if it rains, the grass is slippery.

blocks.heading: Disjunctive Syllogism
blocks.text: Disjunctive Syllogism eliminates a false alternative. p ∨ q ¬p ∴ q I will make tea or read a book. I will not make tea. Therefore, I will read a book.

blocks.heading: Constructive Dilemma
blocks.text: Constructive Dilemma combines two conditionals with a disjunction. p → q; r → s p ∨ r ∴ q ∨ s If Sara wakes early, she exercises. If Lee stays up late, he drinks coffee. Sara wakes early or Lee stays up late. Thus Sara exercises or Lee drinks coffee.

blocks.heading: Simplification
blocks.text: Simplification takes either part of a true conjunction. p ∧ q ∴ p (or ∴ q) The sky is blue and the grass is green. Therefore, the sky is blue.

blocks.heading: Conjunction
blocks.text: The Conjunction rule joins two established statements. p q ∴ p ∧ q Juan drinks coffee. Juan reads a book. Therefore, Juan drinks coffee and reads a book.

blocks.heading: Addition
blocks.text: Addition introduces an inclusive OR. p ∴ p ∨ q It is sunny. Therefore, it is sunny or cloudy. The second alternative need not already be known to be true.

blocks.heading: Double Negation
blocks.text: Double Negation removes or adds two negations without changing truth. p ↔ ¬¬p “It is not the case that DJ did not attend class” has the same truth value as “DJ attended class.”

blocks.heading: Tautologies and equivalence
blocks.text: A tautology is true under every assignment of truth values. For example, p ∨ ¬p is a tautology. Two expressions are logically equivalent when their truth-table columns match. We write A ↔ B as a tautology to express their equivalence.

blocks.heading: Idempotent laws
blocks.text: Repeating a proposition with AND or OR does not change its truth value. p ∨ p ↔ p p ∧ p ↔ p “I will go to school or I will go to school” is equivalent to “I will go to school.” These are the idempotent laws.

blocks.heading: De Morgan’s laws
blocks.text: De Morgan’s laws negate each part and swap AND with OR. ¬(p ∧ q) ↔ (¬p ∨ ¬q) ¬(p ∨ q) ↔ (¬p ∧ ¬q) “Not both” means at least one is false. “Neither” means both are false.

blocks.heading: Commutativity
blocks.text: Commutativity changes order, not truth. p ∧ q ↔ q ∧ p p ∨ q ↔ q ∨ p It applies to AND and OR. A conditional generally cannot be reversed.

blocks.heading: Associativity
blocks.text: Associativity changes grouping, not order. p ∧ (q ∧ r) ↔ (p ∧ q) ∧ r p ∨ (q ∨ r) ↔ (p ∨ q) ∨ r Grouping does not matter when all the connectives are AND, or all are OR.

blocks.heading: Distributive laws
blocks.text:
One connective can distribute over the other.

p ∨ (q ∧ r)
↔ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r)

p ∧ (q ∨ r)
↔ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r)

blocks.heading: Transposition
blocks.text: Transposition replaces a conditional with its contrapositive. Swap the hypothesis and conclusion, and negate both. (p → q) ↔ (¬q → ¬p)

blocks.heading: Material implication
blocks.text: Material implication rewrites a conditional as a disjunction. (p → q) ↔ (¬p ∨ q) When p is false, the conditional is true regardless of q.

blocks.heading: Material equivalence
blocks.text: Material equivalence states both directions of implication. (p ↔ q) ↔ ((p → q) ∧ (q → p)) A biconditional requires both conditionals, not only one.

blocks.heading: Exportation
blocks.text: Exportation rewrites a conjunction in the hypothesis as nested conditionals. ((p ∧ q) → r) ↔ (p → (q → r)) Both forms assert that when p and q hold, r follows.
